tldr: To tackle high-load tasks with severe contact state changes like opening round doorknobs, this paper proposes "TMA," a method that estimates environmental contact properties online from multi-finger tactile history to adapt motor behavior. The authors successfully demonstrated zero-shot sim-to-real transfer on a real-world, full-sized humanoid robot.
hero_caption: Overall architecture of the proposed TMA framework. (a) Integration of a fixed locomotion controller with an upper-body manipulation policy, (b) cone-coordinate parameterization of force vectors based on the friction cone, (c) two-stage training with an oracle policy using privileged information and an adaptation encoder trained on tactile history, and (d) zero-shot deployment pipeline on the physical humanoid robot.
overview:
Research on humanoid loco-manipulation has advanced rapidly. However, most prior work has focused on tasks like pushing down lever handles, where geometric alignment and physical constraints dominate the interaction (geometry-dominant tasks). Opening a door by turning a smooth, round doorknob is a fundamentally harder challenge. It belongs to the "interaction-dominant regime," where the robot must apply sufficient normal force with its fingertips to prevent slip, generate enough torque to overcome strong internal springs, and continuously maintain whole-body balance.

In such tasks, disturbances like friction coefficients and internal door mechanisms (spring stiffness or latch friction) cannot be observed directly through vision or joint encoders. The authors focus on the temporal evolution of fingertip tactile feedback. Unobserved environmental parameters are hidden not merely in the instantaneous contact forces, but in the history of active physical interactions—how contacts respond when the robot applies forces.

This paper proposes Tactile-Driven Motor Adaptation (TMA). It features a tactile representation that embeds the geometric structure of the friction cone, alongside an adaptation encoder that estimates environmental properties online from roughly two seconds of tactile and proprioceptive history. Trained entirely in simulation, the policy was transferred zero-shot to a real humanoid robot (Unitree G1) equipped with non-backdrivable multi-fingered hands. Across four commercial round doorknobs, TMA achieved door opening with success rates that substantially outperformed standard RMA and reactive tactile baselines.
contributions: Formulated round-doorknob opening as a challenging benchmark coupling multi-finger forceful contact control with whole-body stabilization.
Proposed TMA, an adaptation framework that incorporates geometric friction cone inductive biases into tactile representations and estimates environmental properties from active interaction history.
Seamlessly integrated a pretrained whole-body locomotion controller with a tactile manipulation policy, demonstrating zero-shot sim-to-real transfer on a physical humanoid robot.

sections.heading: Beyond geometric alignment: The friction and force challenges of round doorknobs
sections.summary: While traditional humanoid manipulation centers on geometric alignment, tasks like turning round doorknobs require continuous, contact-driven control to handle friction limits and spring counter-torques. To address this, the authors propose TMA, a framework that leverages active tactile history to adapt motor behavior online.
sections.details:
With a lever-style door handle, a robot can often succeed simply by aligning itself geometrically and driving its arm downward. A round doorknob is completely different. It operates in an "interaction-dominant regime" where the robot must carefully place its fingertips, distribute normal forces, and generate frictional torque that overcomes internal return springs without slipping.

The core difficulty of this task is that critical parameters, such as friction coefficients and latch spring stiffness, are not directly observable from vision or joint proprioception. A secure grasp and a state on the verge of slipping look virtually identical in terms of visual appearance and joint angles. Therefore, tactile sensors that directly measure fingertip contact responses are essential.

However, reactive policies that inspect only instantaneous tactile readings are insufficient. Identical instantaneous forces can yield different slip margins or mechanism responses depending on prior motions. To overcome this, the authors developed Tactile-Driven Motor Adaptation (TMA), which accumulates contact history to actively infer physical environment properties and adapt motor commands.

The authors demonstrated that a policy trained purely in simulation transfers zero-shot to a physical system—a Unitree G1 humanoid with BrainCo Revo2 multi-fingered hands—successfully opening four different commercial round doorknobs.

sections.heading: How does this differ from existing whole-body control and tactile sim-to-real?
sections.summary: While humanoid whole-body loco-manipulation and tactile sim-to-real have advanced, most prior efforts focus on lumped end-effector forces or binary contact detection. This work sets itself apart by capturing 3D contact force vectors at each fingertip and leveraging their temporal evolution for motor adaptation.
sections.details:
Learning loco-manipulation has increasingly relied on imitation learning from teleoperation or reinforcement learning in large-scale simulators. While recent works address balancing under heavy external loads, most treat interaction as lumped wrenches at the end-effector or adapt via joint torques. They do not address the complex distribution and regulation of individual contact forces across multiple fingertips.

Meanwhile, tactile sim-to-real transfer has achieved success in door opening and in-hand manipulation. However, many existing methods reduce tactile feedback to binary contact signals or scalar force magnitudes, discarding directional force information. Other approaches use Rapid Motor Adaptation (RMA) architectures to estimate latent physical properties from history, but they rely predominantly on joint proprioception.

For electric multi-fingered hands with high gear ratios and low backdrivability, joint angles barely deflect when external contact forces change. Consequently, proprioception-only RMA struggles. This work breaks through this barrier by parameterizing 3D fingertip force vectors (normal force and shear direction/magnitude) in a physically meaningful representation and exploiting their temporal history.

sections.heading: Physical modeling and problem formulation for the round doorknob task
sections.summary: The full process—a floating-base humanoid turning a spring-loaded doorknob, retracting the latch, and pushing the door open—is formulated as a POMDP. Local fingertip 3D contact forces and the door's physical constraints are formally defined.
sections.details:
### III-A 1 Coordinate Frames and Door Mechanism Model
Let $\{P\}$ denote the robot pelvis frame and $\{W\}$ the world frame. The doorknob has radius $r_K$ and axis $\mathbf{d}_{\{PK\}}$, parameterized by door hinge angle $\theta^D$ and knob rotation angle $\theta^K$. The knob incorporates a return spring exerting counter-torque determined by stiffness $k_K$ and preload $\tau_K^0$. To open the door, the knob must be turned past a release threshold $\theta_{\mathrm{rel}}$ to fully retract the latch.

### III-A 2 Robot Configuration and Action Space
The robot's 41 degrees of freedom $\mathbf{q} \in \mathbb{R}^{41}$ are partitioned into manipulation joints $\mathbf{q}^m \in \mathbb{R}^{13}$ (7-DoF right arm + 6-DoF right hand), locomotion joints $\mathbf{q}^l \in \mathbb{R}^{15}$ (12-DoF legs + 3-DoF waist), and held-posture joints $\mathbf{q}^h \in \mathbb{R}^{13}$ (left arm and hand). The manipulation policy outputs joint position delta commands $\mathbf{a}$.

### III-A 3 Fingertip Tactile Sensing
Local frames $\{T_i\}$ are attached to the tips of the thumb, index, middle, and ring fingers ($n_f=4$). The $+Z$ axis aligns with the outward pad normal. Sensor output is a 3D force vector $\mathbf{f}_i = [f_i^x, f_i^y, f_i^z]^T$, where $f_i^z > 0$ represents compressive normal force, and $f_i^x, f_i^y$ are signed shear forces along the pad tangent plane.

### III-B Problem Formulation
The task is modeled as a finite-horizon Partially Observable Markov Decision Process (POMDP). The deployed policy $\pi$ is trained via reinforcement learning to maximize cumulative reward, using observation history $\mathbf{o}_{0:t}$ to infer unobserved environmental properties.

captions.F2: Kinematic and mechanism model of the articulated door. It consists of the spring-loaded knob rotation axis $\theta^K$, the door hinge axis $\theta^D$, and a latch mechanism coupled to knob rotation. The door panel can only swing open once the knob is rotated past the release threshold $\theta_{\mathrm{rel}}$ to fully retract the latch.

sections.heading: The core of TMA: Friction cone geometry and adaptation via active tactile history
sections.summary: TMA coordinates an upper-body manipulation policy with a lower-body stabilizing locomotion controller while utilizing tactile feedback. It consists of friction-cone-inspired force feature extraction, tactile grasp-gated rewards, two-stage privileged learning, and contact-focused domain randomization.
sections.details:
### IV-A System Architecture
The setup uses a Unitree G1 robot with a BrainCo Revo2 hand. The lower body runs a fixed, robust locomotion controller (commanded with zero velocity), while the upper-body TMA policy controls the arm and hand. Both share proprioceptive observations, such as full-body joint positions, pelvis angular velocity, and projected gravity, allowing the robot to maintain balance against manipulation reaction forces.

### IV-B Tactile-Gated Reward Structure
If the robot opens the door through lucky, ungrounded contacts without engaging its tactile sensors, the adaptation mechanism cannot learn. To prevent this, rotation and door-opening rewards are multiplied by a grasp gate $w_t$. Full reward is granted only when the thumb and at least two opposing finger sensor pads make contact with the knob. This naturally encourages an opposed grasp rich in tactile feedback.

### IV-C Friction Cone-Inspired Tactile Representation
Rather than feeding raw simulated forces directly into a neural network, forces are mapped into a physically meaningful representation. The 3D force vector is clipped at $20\,$N, passed through a first-order low-pass filter (LPF), and converted based on friction cone geometry into a 4D vector $\boldsymbol{\tau}_i$: normal force $n$, cone angle $\alpha$ between the total force vector and normal, and shear direction $(\sin\phi, \cos\phi)$. Designed to avoid angular discontinuities, these 4D features across four fingers yield a 16D tactile observation.

### IV-D Two-Stage Adaptation Framework
- **Stage 1 (Oracle Policy Learning)**: Ground-truth parameters (privileged information) like spring stiffness, friction coefficients, door mass, and hand motor gains are passed to a privileged encoder to extract an 8D latent representation $\mathbf{z}^*_t$. The oracle policy is trained with PPO conditioned on $\mathbf{z}^*_t$ and a short observation history of 3 steps.
- **Stage 2 (Adaptation Encoder Training)**: The oracle policy and privileged encoder are frozen. An adaptation encoder is trained via supervised learning to predict the privileged latent vector from a 100-step deployable observation history (roughly 2 seconds at 50Hz). On the physical robot, this encoder estimates the latent vector $\hat{\mathbf{z}}_t$ online.

### IV-E Contact-Centric Domain Randomization
To bridge the sim-to-real tactile gap, simulation applies aggressive randomization to sensor frame orientation offsets, filter time constants, normal force/shear angle noise, and per-finger contact dropouts. Knob dimensions, spring stiffness, and friction coefficients are also extensively randomized.

captions.F3: Detailed system architecture of TMA. (a) Integration of lower-body locomotion and upper-body manipulation, (b) cone-coordinate parameterization of contact forces using normal force $n$, cone angle $\alpha$, and shear azimuth $\phi$, (c) two-stage training with an oracle policy using privileged information followed by adaptation encoder regression on history, and (d) the deployment inference pipeline on the physical robot.

sections.heading: Hardware validation: Zero-shot success on four commercial doorknobs and ablations
sections.summary: Following simulation training, TMA was evaluated on a physical Unitree G1 robot across four commercial round doorknobs. TMA substantially outperformed RMA and reactive tactile baselines. Simulation ablations further proved that both normal and shear forces are critical to success.
sections.details:
### V-A Simulation Training and Encoder Comparison
Training was conducted in mjlab (MuJoCo-based) across 8,192 parallel environments with physics at 200Hz and policy control at 50Hz. Comparing a GRU against a Temporal Convolutional Network (TConv) for the adaptation encoder, TConv learned faster and achieved a slightly higher final success rate (80% vs 78%), and was thus chosen for deployment.

### V-B Simulation Ablations
The authors evaluated variations of tactile inputs: the full cone representation (TMA), binary contact masks, normal-force-only, and shear-force-only. The full representation achieved overwhelmingly superior grasp and door opening success rates. Binary contacts and normal-only feedback could grasp the knob but failed to regulate the shear forces needed for rotation. Shear-only feedback lacked normal support, performing worst. This confirms that coordinating both normal force and shear direction is vital for forceful interaction.

### V-C Real-World Evaluation
Hardware experiments tested four commercial doorknobs: tapered (Knob 1), spherical (Knob 2), flat disk (Knob 3), and olive-shaped (Knob 4), with 10 trials per knob. Initial robot stand positions and table heights were randomized to assess robustness.
- **TMA (Proposed)**: Successfully completed the full sequence—from grasping to turning and pushing open—across the vast majority of trials on all four knobs.
- **Reactive Policy**: Detected contact but slipped during rotation, failing to open the door.
- **RMA (Tactile-free, proprioception-only)**: Hands drifted and lifted off the knob almost immediately upon contact, failing to maintain a grasp. This highlighted the fundamental failure of joint-based estimation on hands with low backdrivability.

captions.F4: Execution sequences of TMA on the real humanoid robot. From top to bottom: tapered (Knob 1), spherical (Knob 2), disk (Knob 3), and olive-shaped (Knob 4) commercial doorknobs. The robot reliably executes the entire approach, grasp, rotate, and open sequence across all knob geometries.
captions.F7: Typical failure modes of baseline methods on hardware. Top: The reactive tactile policy establishes contact but cannot regulate force profiles properly, failing to open the door. Bottom: RMA slips off the knob surface immediately after contact, unable to sustain contact.

sections.heading: Lessons from interaction-dominant manipulation and future directions
sections.summary: The experiments reveal three key insights: the necessity of tactile sensing on non-backdrivable hands, the identification of physical properties through active contact history, and physical limitations imposed by Coulomb friction limits. The results demonstrate the power of tactile adaptation in forceful, interaction-dominant tasks.
sections.details:
The findings yield three primary lessons regarding humanoid physical interaction:

1. **Tactile sensing is mandatory for non-backdrivable hands**: Industrial and humanoid hands use high gear ratios that lack backdrivability, meaning external interaction forces do not register on joint encoders. Proprioceptive adaptation methods like standard RMA fail, making direct fingertip contact sensing essential.
2. **The necessity of active interaction history**: A single instantaneous tactile frame is inherently ambiguous. Unobserved parameters like friction limits and spring stiffness only reveal themselves through temporal changes—observing how contact forces evolve as the hand applies motion.
3. **Physical limits of fingertip pads and wear effects**: As dictated by Coulomb friction ($s \leq \mu n$), achievable torque is bounded by the friction coefficient $\mu$ and normal force $n$. During experiments, pad rubber wear and surface damage led to steep drops in success, proving that physical pad conditions are critical since fingertips serve as both sensors and mechanical force transmitters.

Future work includes extending TMA to a broader range of interaction-dominant tasks beyond doorknobs and incorporating longer temporal contexts.

takeaways: For tasks like round-doorknob opening where friction and force regulation dictate success, measuring 3D contact force vectors is essential, as vision and joint angles alone are insufficient.
On hands with low backdrivability, proprioception-based adaptation (standard RMA) fails; online adaptation driven by multi-finger tactile history (TMA) provides the missing physical feedback.
Decomposing contact forces into friction-cone-inspired coordinates (normal force, cone angle, and shear direction) preserves physical meaning while enabling robust reinforcement learning.
Loosely coupling a fixed whole-body locomotion controller for balance with a tactile-adaptive upper-body manipulation policy achieves stable sim-to-real transfer for complex loco-manipulation.
limitations: Performance depends heavily on the physical friction coefficient of fingertip pads; rubber wear or tearing breaches friction limits and leads to task failure.
Doorknob pose estimation relies on AprilTags, meaning the system does not yet integrate end-to-end real-world vision feedback.
Generalization across wider contact tasks—such as pulling doors open or handling heavy industrial latches—remains unverified.
